evidence: Gell. 1.23.4: mōs anteā senātōribus Rōmae fuit
terms.comment: Before some time in the past, often answered by posteā or nunc: hunc audiēbant anteā, nunc praesentem vident (Cic. Imp. Pomp., Lewis & Short). Atticus objected to anteā where prius was meant (Cic. Att. 15.13, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Gell. 16.3.2: cum antehāc semper edundī fuerit adpetēns, nunc …
terms.comment: Before the present moment, usually set against nunc. Lewis & Short calls anteā relative (before any time spoken of) and antehāc demonstrative (before now), though Plautus and Sallust also use antehāc of an earlier time in the past.
Earlier than something else that is named or meant; with quam, before (see before, the conjunction).

evidence: Cic. Sen. 19: annō ante mē cēnsōrem
terms.comment: As an adverb mostly with a measure of time: paulō ante, a little earlier; multīs ante annīs, many years before (see before, of a time).

phrases.latin: mōs anteā senātōribus Rōmae fuit in cūriam cum praetextātīs fīliīs introīre
phrases.english: it used to be the custom at Rome for senators to go into the senate house with their young sons

phrases.latin: cum antehāc semper edundī fuerit adpetēns, nunc post imperātam inediam triduī omnis ejus adpetītiō prīstina ēlanguerit
phrases.english: though he had always been fond of his food before, now, after the three days’ fast he was ordered, all his old appetite has died away

phrases.latin: ō suāvis anima! quāle tē dīcam bonum antehāc fuisse, tālēs cum sint reliquiae?
phrases.english: O sweet soul! How good must I say you were before, when your leavings are like this?

sources: Lewis & Short: antea · Lewis & Short: antehac · Lewis & Short: prius · Lewis & Short: ante
